In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of affective dysregulation in patients with BPD and SoDs.
the nature and inter-relations of dysfunctional under- and/or overregulation of emotions in BPD and in SoD.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of childhood trauma, PTSD, and/or CPTSD is not disorder specific, but that the type of traumatic experiences and associated dysfunctional affect regulation and dissociation are disorder specific.
dysfunctional affect regulation is common in BPD, SoD, and BPD+ SoD and is associated with childhood trauma and CPTSD.
affect dysregulation may be a core feature of BPD and SoDs but is not a disorder-specific feature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current findings provide support for the existence of different subtypes of BPD and SoDs that can be distinguished by the nature of their dysfunctional affect regulation.
dysfunctional regulation of affect and somatic and psychoform dissociations in BPD and in SoD can be understood as a consequence of early childhood trauma exposure and CPT.
dysfunctional regulation of affect and dissociation are not specific to either BPD or SoD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are three qualitatively distinct forms of dysfunctional affect regulation in BPD and in SoD, namely inhibitory, excitatatory, and combined states.
the nature and severity of dysfunctional affect regulation, and its association with CPTSD, is disorder specific and is best understood in the context of childhood TPC.
the clinical presentation of BPD and SoDs is not uniform.
